body:
## The remedy above has the same failure mode, so it is worth naming here

Of the three shapes, one is countable and two need judgment. The five-to-nothing
ratio in shape 3 can be shown to have been checked. Shapes 1 and 2 cannot.

Put all three into a checklist and it does not stay a three-item checklist. It
becomes a one-item checklist with two sentences of preamble, because the
countable one is the only one anybody can demonstrate having done. A check whose
satisfaction cannot be demonstrated loses to one whose can, even when the
demonstrable one matters less. That is this issue's own defect, one level up.

The fix is not to invent numbers for shapes 1 and 2. A metric invented to
protect a judgment becomes the thing people satisfy, which is where this
started.

The fix is to ask for a written answer rather than a pass mark: one sentence per
shape, in the words of the change under review. A sentence is evidence that the
question was asked, without pretending the answer is a measurement. Somebody who
cannot write the sentence has not looked.

## A third tooling instance, and its mechanism is distinct

The two in *The same family outside tests* are both **commands that cannot report failure**. This one is different and worth naming separately: a **pipeline that reports the wrong command's verdict**. It does not merely hide a red. It manufactures a green.

It happened in one line, twice, in two different ways.

### First: a redirect that hid the reason

```sh
echo "== the laws =="; bash scripts/laws.sh >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "lawsscript_exit=$?"
```

This reports `lawsscript_exit=1` and nothing else. The exit code is honest, and it is useless: there is no way to tell a real red from a script invoked wrongly, so the reading is "probably my mistake" and the step gets dismissed. A check that reports only a number teaches you to distrust the number.

### Then: a pipe that reported the tail's verdict

Re-running it to see the reason:

```sh
bash scripts/laws.sh 2>&1 | tail -25; echo laws_exit=$?
```

This printed a screen full of `--- FAIL` and then, underneath it, `laws_exit=0`. `$?` is `tail`'s status, and `tail` succeeded. Both law failures were real, both were caused by the change under test, and the line claiming to check them declared success directly below the evidence.

This is the nastier shape. The exit-zero-always command leaves a green where a check should be; this one puts a green *underneath the failure itself*, and in a long chain the summary line is what gets read.

### What replaced it

```sh
bash scripts/laws.sh > /tmp/laws.log 2>&1; LAWS=$?
echo "laws_exit=$LAWS"
echo "law FAIL lines: $(grep -c '^FAIL\|^--- FAIL' /tmp/laws.log)"
grep -n '^--- FAIL\|^FAIL' /tmp/laws.log | head -20
```

Three properties, and each one is doing separate work:

1. The status is captured **before** anything else runs, so no later command can overwrite it.
2. The output goes to a file rather than through a pipe, so reading it cannot change what is reported.
3. The **content** is checked independently of the status. A FAIL count is a second, differently-sourced witness, which is what catches the case where the status is wrong.

The third is the general form. Where a step's status and its output are two separate signals, read both; where they disagree, that disagreement is information.

### The same shape in a test filter

A related instance, same night, different surface: a chain step ran

```sh
go test -run 'TestA|TestB|TestC|TestD|TestE|TestF' ./internal/session/
```

against a file that by then held seven tests. The seventh was not in the pattern. It reported `ok`.

**A named test that did not run is indistinguishable from a named test that passed**, in every artifact anybody downstream reads. There is no FAIL to count here, so the second witness has to be the enumeration itself: have the step print the tests it actually ran and compare that against the list it was told to run, so the two copies cannot drift. `go test -v` and a `grep -c '^--- PASS'` is enough.

### Why it belongs in this issue

The review question in the body applies unchanged, pointed at a proof step rather than a test:

**What would this step print if the thing it checks were broken?**

If the answer is "the same thing it prints now", it is not a check. All three instances answer that question the same way, and a reader who has only met the exit-zero-always shape will not recognise the pipeline one when they write it, because the exit code in that one is doing exactly what the shell documents.

## Shape 4, and it should be read first: a reading whose failure mode is a plausible value

The three shapes above are about CHECKS. This one is about READINGS, and it is
worse than any of them, because the other three produce something a careful
reader can see is wrong. This one produces a number that passes every sanity
check you could write.

Example, observed 2026-09-20. Four cell spend ledgers were totalled by summing a
named field across the rows of each file. The reader returned 0.0 for all four.
There was no error, no non-zero exit, no missing file and no empty input. The
field name was simply wrong, so every row contributed nothing.

Zero is a legitimate value. A cell that has spent nothing reads zero. Nothing
downstream can tell that sum from a true one.

It was caught only because four-for-four zero was implausible against four cells
known to be actively writing. Had one of them been idle, or had a single cell
been checked instead of four, the number would have been believed and quoted.
THE DETECTOR WAS THE POPULATION, NOT THE READER.

What the replacement asserts: not a better field name, which only moves the same
failure. A SECOND WITNESS THAT CANNOT BE ZERO. Read the field and the row count
together and disagree loudly on a sum with no rows behind it. More generally,
pair any aggregate with a count of what went into it, so that "nothing was
found" and "everything found was nothing" cannot produce the same output.

## The remedy under all four

Three separate instances of one fix have now turned up in a single day: a sum
paired with its row count; a number stated in the same sentence as the list it
counts, so the two cannot drift; and a question asked of a surface paired with
what the surface reports. In each case the fix is the same move: make the two
copies of one fact impossible to write independently, so that disagreement is a
failure rather than a discrepancy nobody compares.

That is worth naming, because it is also the defect these surfaces had in the
first place. Two readers of one question that never consult the same book.

## The review question has a second form, for claims rather than code

The question above, asked of a test, is: what would have to be broken for this
to fail?

The same question asked of a STATEMENT in a review, a commit message or a design
note is: what would be different if this were not true?

If the answer is "nothing", the statement is not carrying the weight it is being
quoted for, however true it is. This matters because a true statement passes
every check in this issue. A false claim can be measured against the world. A
true one that implies more than it establishes cannot, and it will be repeated
accurately by careful people until something downstream depends on the part it
never said.

Worth asking of any sentence that closes a question rather than opening one.

## Correction to shape 4's example, and the true cause is a better instance

I wrote above that the reader returned 0.0 for all four files because "the field
name was simply wrong". That was a guess made at the time and it is not what
happened. The field name was right.

What actually happened: the reader wrapped its whole read in a bare
`try: ... except: pass`, so a failure BEFORE any row was parsed produced the
same output as a file full of zero-cost rows. Re-run with the exception surfaced
and a row count beside the sum, the same four files read:

```
c369 rows=121 usd=1.67
c370 rows=47  usd=0.32
c372 rows=52  usd=0.60
c373 rows=54  usd=0.57
```

So the shape stands and the example is now sharper than the one I gave. The
reader did not misread the data. IT FAILED, and its failure was reported as a
legitimate value. A wrong field name at least reads every row and finds nothing
in each; a swallowed exception can stop before the first row and still answer
with a number.

The prescribed replacement catches this version too, and is what produced the
table above: pair the aggregate with a count of what went into it. `rows=0`
beside `usd=0.00` is a failure that announces itself. `usd=0.00` alone is not.

Worth adding to the shape: a bare `except: pass` around a read is this defect in
its purest form, because it converts every possible failure into the reader's
most plausible output.

## One instance of shape 4 has a syntax, so it can have a rule

Shape 4 is not detectable in general. A reading whose failure produces a
plausible value can be written a hundred ways and most of them need judgement to
spot. But ONE FORM of it has a syntax, exactly and without judgement, so a rule
can have that form.

Read this as catching one instance, NOT as covering the shape. A rule sold as
covering shape 4 becomes the reason nobody looks for the rest of it, which is
the trap this issue is about in the first place.

### The detectable form

A catch-all around the READ ITSELF, as opposed to around one row's parse. The
distinction is what makes the rule precise rather than noisy:

```python
# The defect. A failure to open, or to iterate, answers with the same value as
# a file full of zero-cost rows.
try:
    for line in open(path):
        total += json.loads(line).get("usd", 0)
except:
    pass

# Not the defect. The catch-all is inside the loop, so a bad row is skipped,
# every other row is still counted, and a failure to OPEN still raises.
for line in open(path):
    try:
        total += json.loads(line).get("usd", 0)
    except:
        continue
```

The rule: a bare `except` (or `except Exception`) whose `try` block contains the
open or the iteration, in code that returns an aggregate. Flag it. The fix is to
move the catch inside the loop, or to let the failure raise.

### The Go form in this repo

The same defect here is a discarded error on a read that feeds an aggregate: a
returned error assigned to `_`, or swallowed into a zero return, on a path whose
result is then summed, counted or compared. The current gates are
`go vet ./...` and the formatting check, and neither catches it, because
neither is wrong about anything it was built for.

### Why a rule is worth it here and nowhere else in this issue

Shapes 1 to 3 need judgement and a rule catching a third of them would restart
the same false comfort one level up. This one does not need judgement. The cost
of the rule is a lint entry, and what it buys is that the single purest form of
the defect stops being possible to write by accident. Everything else in this
issue stays a review question, and should.

### One closure worth recording

The replacement prescribed for shape 4, pairing an aggregate with a count of
what went into it, found the defect that motivated it, on its first use, without
anyone going looking. `rows=0` beside `usd=0.00` announces a failure.
`usd=0.00` alone does not.

issue.body:
Three reads in `internal/store` report a failure as a legitimate, favourable
value. Each one still produces a number, so nothing downstream can tell a
measurement from a failure to measure.

> ### Before you write the obvious patch
>
> **The obvious fix can stop a person being consulted.** Excluding an undecodable
> row removes one from `Different` and one from `N` together, and
> `ExpectedRegret = Different/N × MeanReworkCost` therefore strictly falls.
> With `VOIMinSamples = 8` and `VOIRegretThreshold = 0.05`:
>
> | a category of 9 answered rows, default accepted every time, one row undecodable | `N` | `Different` | regret | `ShouldAsk` |
> | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
> | today | 9 | 1 | 0.111 | **asks** |
> | after the obvious fix | 8 | 0 | 0.000 | **does not ask** |
>
> The sample floor does not rescue it; `N` is still 8. All four sites below are on
> the road that decides whether a person is asked. The worked reasoning, the
> opposite-direction effect through the sample floor, and three candidate answers
> are in the comments.
>
> **And doing nothing is also a choice with a cost.** Today the statistic is
> silently wrong, and an undecodable row is counted as a person having disagreed
> with a default they were never shown to have seen. The fix is delicate and the
> status quo is not safe. Whoever takes this is choosing between two wrongs with
> their eyes open, not deciding whether to disturb something that works.

## What happened

No log line, and that is the defect. Each of these fails silently by
construction, so there is nothing to quote from a screen. The evidence is the
code, read at `dev@3d3b7542b` on 2026-09-20.

**One.** `QuestionCategoryStats` in `internal/store/meta.go` (search
`question category stats`):

```go
var options []QuestionOption
_ = json.Unmarshal([]byte(encoded), &options)
stat.N++
if questionAnswerMatchesDefault(resolution, offered, options) {
	stat.Accepted++
} else {
	stat.Different++
}
```

A failed decode leaves `options` nil. `questionAnswerMatchesDefault` (same file,
search `func questionAnswerMatchesDefault`) then skips its only loop and returns
false unless the answer and the offered default are string equal, so the row is
counted `Different`. A row that cannot be decoded is reported as a person having
disagreed with the default.

**Two.** `measureCorrectionStyle` in `internal/store/traits.go` (search
`measureCorrectionStyle`) makes the identical discarded decode, and its result
chooses `continue` against `total += right.Sub(left)`. There a failed decode
changes a duration total rather than a count.

**Three, and the worst of them.** `meanCategoryReworkCost` in
`internal/store/meta.go` (search `func (s *Store) meanCategoryReworkCost`):

```go
rows, err := s.db.Query(`SELECT session_id, answer_message_seq, ...`)
if err != nil {
	return 0
}
```

A query failure is reported as a mean rework cost of ZERO. Not an error, not a
sentinel. Zero cost is not merely plausible here, it is FAVOURABLE: the reading
fails in the direction that flatters the thing being measured.

## Replication

**Deterministic (no model).** NOT YET RUN. Written from the code read above and
offered as a recipe rather than as an observation, which is why no output is
quoted. Anybody with the repo can run it:

1. In `internal/store`, open a test store and record an answered durable
   question in a category, with a real options list and a resolution that
   matches the offered default. `Store.AskQuestion` is the exported recorder.
2. Overwrite that row's `options` column with a value the decoder rejects, which
   is what schema drift, truncation, or a value written by an older build
   produces in the field.
3. Call `Store.QuestionCategoryStats` for that category.

Expected today: `N` is 1 and the row lands in `Different`, although the person
took the default. Correct behaviour: the decode failure is visible, by error or
by exclusion from the sample, and never by silent reclassification.

For the third defect, point the store at an unreadable or locked database and
call the mean cost path. Expected today: `0`, indistinguishable from a category
that genuinely cost nothing.

**Field (real models).** No special conditions. Any deployment whose
`agent_questions.options` column holds a value this build's decoder rejects is
already producing these numbers, and has no way to know.

## Where

`internal/store/meta.go`: `QuestionCategoryStats`,
`questionAnswerMatchesDefault`, `meanCategoryReworkCost`.
`internal/store/traits.go`: `measureCorrectionStyle`.

## The fix

A read that fails must not answer with a value that means something else.

For the two decodes, the decode error is either returned, or the row is counted
as undecodable and excluded from the classification, with the excluded count
carried on the result so a reader can see the sample was not whole. Silently
recategorising it is the one option that must go.

For the mean cost, a query failure is an error to the caller. If a zero is
genuinely wanted for a category with no measurable rows, that case is distinct
from a broken query and must be spelled differently, because a caller cannot
act on a number that means both.

The general rule, which is the point of all three: pair an aggregate with a
count of what went into it, so that "nothing was found" and "the read failed"
cannot produce the same output.

## Acceptance

- **e2e:** through the real door that surfaces these figures, a category
  containing one undecodable options row reports its sample as incomplete rather
  than reporting that row as a disagreement, with the exact counts asserted.
- **e2e:** the control, a category whose rows all decode, reports the same
  numbers it reports today, so the change is visible only where the data is bad.
- **Unit:** `questionAnswerMatchesDefault` is never reached with options that
  failed to decode; the structural law is that every path which decodes
  `options` either handles the error or excludes the row.
- The change entry's `invalidates` names what people believed before: that these
  counts describe the rows, rather than describing the rows that happened to
  decode.

## Shape

These are three instances of one shape, catalogued in #1306 as a reading whose
failure produces a plausible value. Found by a five minute look while writing
that issue, not by an audit; the rest of the tree has not been checked, and no
total should be inferred from three.

body:
## Shape 5: a test that greps the source instead of calling the decision

It reads the source file as text and asserts that certain strings are present.
It never runs the code. It asserts that the source LOOKS like the fix, so it
survives every mutation that does not disturb the text.

This is not shape 1 in another costume. A test that pins a string RUNS the code
and asserts the wrong thing about what came out. This one does not execute the
thing it guards at all. The remedies differ too, which is the better
discriminator: shape 1 is fixed by pressing the key and asserting the effect,
and this is fixed by extracting the decision until there is something to call.

### The example, demonstrated rather than reasoned

A guard check named `B: an unreadable box is treated as over limit`. As written,
it read a launcher script into a string and asserted that two substrings were
both present: `unreadable box` and `_over = True`. No call, no state, no
decision exercised.

The mutation, run both ways by its author. In a temporary copy, the branch
`elif a.door == "task":` was changed to `elif False:`, which restores the
fail-open exactly: an unreadable box stops being treated as over limit. Both
greped strings survive that edit untouched, because the comment above the branch
and the assignment inside it are both still there. The guard suite was run
against the mutated copy and PASSED, exit 0, every check green. After the check
was replaced with a real call, the same mutation makes the suite exit 1 with
three named red checks including that one. Before and after, both observed.

### The tell, which is the practical half

The author did not choose to grep. They greped because there was nothing to
call: the decision was smeared across three branches in one path, plus a fourth
place where the reason string was assembled by a separate conditional that could
disagree with all three. Four places, one decision, nothing callable.

So the tell warns you in advance rather than after: WHEN A TEST WANTS TO GREP,
THE THING IT WANTS TO ASSERT IS NOT REACHABLE AS A CALLABLE. The grep is a
symptom of that, not laziness.

The fix followed the tell. The decision became one function returning its verdict
and its reason together, so that "unreadable means over limit" is true inside it
by construction rather than by three branches agreeing, and the guard calls it.

A third defect fell out on the way, worth recording because it is a fourth shape
in miniature: with the fail-open restored, the mutated copy CRASHED rather than
failing by name, and a crash was not counted as a catch. A suite that cannot say
which guard broke has produced an unreadable red, and an unreadable red gets
rerun until it passes.

### Why this issue needs mechanical parts and not only a review question

The author of that check wrote it about an hour after explaining shape 4 above,
correctly and in their own words, while not confused about any part of it. They
have agreed to this being recorded here.

Understanding a defect shape does not prevent you producing it, because writing
a guard is precisely the moment your attention is on the thing guarded rather
than on the guard. That is the argument for the mechanical parts. Not that
reviewers are careless, which was never true, but that the moment you write a
check is by definition the moment your attention is somewhere else.

## Where the next one will be found

Every tooling defect found while writing this issue lived OUTSIDE the
repository: in ad-hoc chain scripts, launchers, probes and briefs. That surface
has no reviewer, no gate and no test, and it is where the expensive mistakes of
the past week came from. A survey of the Makefile, `scripts/` and
`.github/` for three specific shell shapes (a formatting check reading an exit
code instead of a list, a status reported after a pipe, and a test filter that
can drift from a list of names) found none. `make fmt-check` captures the list
and exits on non-empty, correctly, and every `| grep` in those directories sits
inside a boolean predicate where the pipeline's status is exactly the question
being asked.

That is the honest answer to anyone who reads this and asks why the repo's own
gates caught none of it: they were not pointed at the code that had the bugs.

And the reviewed surface is not clean either. A five minute look, not an audit,
found three live instances of shape 4 in one package, filed as #1309. No total
should be inferred from three, because nobody has checked the rest.

## Where these defects actually live: a survey, with its scope attached

Before proposing that anything in the tree be converted to a safer form, I looked for the three tooling shapes in the tree. **There are none.** That result is more interesting than a list of fixes would have been, and it is worth stating precisely, because a finding quoted without its scope becomes a larger claim than the one that was tested.

### What was looked for, and where

| Defect | Searched | Found |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a `gofmt -l` whose exit code is read | `Makefile`, `scripts/`, `.github/` | 0 |
| a status reported after a pipe (`cmd \| tail; echo $?`) | same | 0 |
| a `-run` pattern listing named tests that can drift from a file | same | 0 |

`make fmt-check` at `Makefile:240` already captures the list and exits on non-empty. It was written in the correct form before any of this came up. Every `| grep` and `| head` in `scripts/` and `.github/` sits inside a boolean predicate, where the pipeline's status **is** the question being asked, which is correct usage rather than the defect.

### The scope, stated so it cannot be widened

That count covers **those three shapes** in **those three directories**. It says nothing about any other way a failure can be discarded, and **nothing about Go source, which was not looked at**. Anyone quoting the number should carry the boundary with it; a scoped finding whose scope travels separately turns into a claim nobody tested. That is the same defect as a check that cannot fail, facing the boundary instead of the content.

### What the zero actually means

All three defects were real, and every instance of all three was in an **ad-hoc chain script written outside the repository** — the scripts we drive proof runs with, which have no reviewer, no gate and no test.

So the gates worked. The defects were in the places the gates do not reach.

That generalises past these three, and it is the reason to write it down while the instances are fresh rather than recalling it later as an impression: the reviewed surface held, and the unreviewed surface had the same defect three times in one night, in three independent sessions, none of which could see the others' scripts. Nobody has to act on it today. It is the kind of thing that is a finding now and an opinion in a month.

issue.title: scripts: three proof steps that could not report failure, in one tested form

repository.name: CodeAF

issue.body:
Three shapes of proof step were each written more than once in this repo's chains, and each is structurally incapable of reporting the failure it is checking for. They were found in one night, each by a different person, each in a different instrument. This is the one written form of all three, to be sourced.

| The shape | Why it cannot fail |
| --- | --- |
| `gofmt -l ./internal; echo "exit=$?"` | `gofmt -l` prints the files it would reformat and **exits 0 either way**. The list is the signal; the exit code never was. |
| `cmd 2>&1 \| tail -25; echo "exit=$?"` | `$?` is `tail`'s status, and `tail` succeeds at reading a failure. This printed `exit=0` underneath a screen of `--- FAIL`. It does not hide a red, it **manufactures a green directly below the evidence**. |
| `go test -run 'TestA\|TestB\|...'` | A `-run` pattern is a second copy of the list of tests in a file. When they drift, `go test` answers a filter matching nothing with `ok`, because from its side nothing failed. **A named test that did not run is indistinguishable from one that passed.** |

`scripts/proof.sh` gives each one a written form: `fmt_check` reads the list; `step` captures its command's status before anything else can run, keeps output in a file rather than a pipe, and counts failures from that file as a second witness sourced differently from the status; `run_tests` compares the names asked for against the tests that reported, and names every one that reported nothing.

That last point is deliberate. A guard whose satisfaction can only be shown as a tick eventually becomes a tick, so the failure is loud and specific in the same line: both counts, and the names.

## The acceptance is the failing arm

`internal/ci/prooflib_test.go` runs each function **twice**: once where the thing it checks is sound, once where it is broken. Each broken arm also pins what the plain command says about the same situation, because that is the entire argument for the function existing.

| Test | What the plain command says | What the library says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TestRunTestsCatchesANameThatReportedNothing` | `go test -run '^(TestAlpha\|TestGamma)$'` on a package holding only Alpha and Beta reports **ok, exit 0** | `asked=2  reported=1`, names `TestGamma`, exit 1 |
| `TestFmtCheckFailsOnAFileGofmtWouldRewrite` | `gofmt -l` lists the file and **exits 0** | prints the list, `gofmt=DIRTY`, exit 1 |
| `TestStepReportsTheCommandsOwnStatusAndNotAPipesStatus` | the pipeline reports **`exit=0`** for a command that exited 3 | `probe_exit=3`, `probe_FAIL_lines=1`, exit 3 |

A guard against invisible failure that has only ever been seen passing is the thing it was written to prevent, wearing its own name.

### Those three assertions are the library's expiry date, not belt and braces

Read them again as a set. Each one says *the hazard is still real*.

Most guards never find out when the thing they guard against gets fixed. The upstream tool changes, the hazard goes away, and the guard lives on as cargo that everybody routes around and nobody dares delete, because by every signal available no one can tell what it was for.

This one announces it. If `go test` ever stops reporting `ok` on a filter naming a test that does not exist, if `gofmt -l` ever starts exiting non-zero on a non-empty list, or if a pipeline ever starts carrying the failing command's status, the corresponding test goes red — and **that red means the library's reason for existing has gone**, not that the library is broken. The failure message in each says so in those terms: *this test is no longer about a silent pass*, *this test proves nothing*, *this test is about nothing*.

The same idea runs through the third mutation control. Putting `step`'s command back behind a pipe reproduces the original defect on demand, so the bug that motivated the library is now permanently a test of it.

## Proof

Fresh clone of `436933a6d` on the test box.

| Step | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `gofmt -l` (the list) | empty |
| `go build ./...` | exit 0 |
| `go vet ./internal/ci/` | exit 0 |
| the five new tests, verbosely | 5 PASS, 0 FAIL, exit 0 |
| whole `./internal/ci/` | ok, exit 0, 0 FAIL lines |
| `scripts/laws.sh` | exit 0, 0 FAIL lines |

**Three mutation controls on the library itself**, each restored green afterwards. Breaking the library must make its own tests red, or the tests are decoration:

1. `run_tests`' count comparison removed → `TestRunTestsCatchesANameThatReportedNothing` red: *the library agreed with the plain command and reported success*.
2. `fmt_check` made to read the exit code instead of the list → red: *an unformatted tree was reported clean*.
3. `step`'s command put back behind a pipe → red: *step answered 0, not the command's own 3*. That is the original defect, reproduced on demand.

## Scope

**No caller is converted here, and there is none to convert.** A survey for these three shapes across `Makefile`, `scripts/` and `.github/` found zero instances: `make fmt-check` was already written in the correct form, no shipped chain reports a status after a pipe, and no `-run` pattern lists named tests that could drift from a file. Every instance was in an ad-hoc chain script written outside the repository.

That count covers those three shapes in those three directories and claims nothing about any other way a failure can be discarded, and nothing about Go source, which was not looked at. The scope is stated in the entry and in the file header for the same reason everything else here is written twice-proof: a finding whose boundary travels separately from it becomes a claim nobody tested. The survey and what the zero means are in the issue below.

**So these functions may have no caller, and that is not a reason to delete the file.** Its standing value is the test: three assertions about how the tooling behaves that our proof chains depend on, which run on every pull request whether or not a line of it is ever sourced.

Nothing a person using this program can see changes, so no manual page is owed. The test-shaped members of the same family, the review question, and the survey with its scope are in the issue titled "Tests that cannot fail" (#1306).

body:
## The same defect one level up: a verdict that cannot fail either

A worked instance from tonight, paid for rather than imagined, and the level it
sits at is the point.

A cell produced a correct change and reported its verification as:

```
declared check `go test ./internal/session -run TestPresenceAskReason` exits 0
```

No test of that name exists in that package. Verified twice, independently, in
the cell's own tree: nothing matches, nothing shares the prefix, and the tests it
actually wrote are named differently. A `-run` pattern matching no test cannot
fail on behaviour. The only thing it can catch is the package failing to
compile. The check asserted nothing about the change it was checking and
reported exit 0 as proof.

The brief's declared check was the whole package. The run record contains no
`go test` line at all, so it was never run rather than merely unrecorded.

Now the level that matters. The harness that judged this run is the cell
rig's settle step in `task-run.sh`, and it recorded `findings_ok: true`,
`findings_run_present: true`, `run_record_stray: []`. It looked at this and
called it clean. Named deliberately: an anonymous example invites every reader
to assume it was somebody else's harness, which is the comfort this issue is
about.

THE VERDICT WAS NOT WEAK, IT WAS ABSENT, and the distinction matters to whoever
fixes it. `findings_ok` answers a different question entirely, whether a
plan-store result exists and whether the tree is free of stray findings files.
Nothing was ever wired from it to the declared check. So there is no broken
assertion to find. Somebody going looking for one will waste the afternoon.
The verdict is a check that cannot fail for this defect, sitting one level above
the check that cannot fail.

It was caught because a person read the diff. Nothing in the automated chain
would have.

### Two more mechanically detectable instances

Both are exact, neither needs judgement, and they belong beside the bare-except
rule above as things a rule can have:

1. **The declared command was never executed.** Assert that the command a run
   declares as its check appears in that run's record. A check nobody ran and a
   check that passed produce the same verdict today.
2. **A `-run` pattern that matches nothing.** `go test -run` with no matching
   test still exits 0. Assert the matched test count is nonzero, which the tool
   itself will tell you. This is the test-filter form of the same disease: a
   selector that silently selects nothing reports the same success as a suite
   that passed.

As with the bare-except rule, these catch two instances, not the shape. The
shape stays a review question.

### What this instance is actually evidence for

The author of that check understood this issue. So did the harness that cleared
it. Neither knowing the shape nor automating around it was sufficient, and they
failed in the same direction on the same night, which is the argument for having
both the mechanical parts and the review question rather than choosing between
them.

## The written forms exist

#1308 carries the tested implementations for three of the shell-side shapes
above, including the `-run` filter that matches nothing. The instance logged in
its thread is the one described earlier here: an automated run reporting
`go test ./internal/session -run TestPresenceAskReason` as passing, against a
package with no test of that name.

Recorded here because the two issues answer different questions and both are
needed. #1308 is what to write instead, for the cases that have a written form.
This one is what to look for, for everything that does not.

## What the shapes have in common, offered as a prediction rather than a summary

Every shape above, and the tooling instances in the last section, is ONE OUTPUT
WITH TWO MEANINGS, where the failing meaning is the silent one and the
succeeding meaning is what everything downstream assumes.

A green is "the assertion held" and "the assertion never ran". Zero is "nothing
was spent" and "I failed before the first row". Exit 1 is "the tests failed" and
"the box was busy". In each case the two meanings share a representation, so no
reader downstream can separate them, and the one that gets assumed is the one
that costs nothing to assume.

This is offered because of what it PREDICTS, not because it ties the list
together. The five shapes tell you how to review a test you are already looking
at. The pattern tells you where to go looking, and it names a specific place:
AN ERROR PATH THAT RETURNS A VALUE IN THE SAME DOMAIN AS THE SUCCESS PATH. Those
are findable without judgement. `return 0`, `return ""`, `return nil, nil`, a
bare `except: pass`, a swallowed `err` in a function whose result is a number.

Four instances in this tree and its tooling, each read at
`3d3b7542b` or in the linked issue rather than recalled:

- `internal/store/meta.go:488` and `:502`. `meanCategoryReworkCost` returns `0`
  when the query fails and `0` again when `rows.Close()` fails. Zero is a
  legitimate mean rework cost. A third at `:498` drops any row whose `Scan`
  fails, so a partial read and a complete one produce the same kind of answer.
  Filed as #1309.
- `cmd/codeaf-suite-lock/main.go:126`. Contention returns `1`. `go test` also
  returns `1` for a red. The stderr text distinguishes them and the exit code
  does not, so any runner keyed on the code reads "the box was busy" as "the
  work is wrong". Filed as #1320.
- A `-run` pattern matching no test. `go test` prints `ok` and is correct to:
  a filter matching nothing is a run with nothing in it. What the step could
  ever have caught was compilation. #1308 carries the form that objects,
  comparing the names asked for against the names that reported.
- Shape 4 in this issue, which I hit myself: a reader whose exception handler
  produced a plausible total, so the number was wrong and nothing downstream
  could question it.

## The reason this is a comment and not a rewrite of the body

A frame is less demonstrable than any of the five shapes, and this issue has
already been bitten once by the demonstrable crowding out the rest: shape 3 is
countable and became the only one anybody could be shown to have done. A pattern
that explains all five is the extreme case of that, quotable without doing
anything. If it starts being cited in place of the shapes, it has made this
issue worse, and the shapes are what a reviewer can actually apply to a diff in
front of them.

The honest division: use the shapes to review what is in front of you, use the
pattern to decide where to look next, and do not let the second stand in for the
first.

## A positive example, because every instance above is a failure

This issue and its comment so far describe only the bad version. Here is an
artefact in this repository that already does the thing right, and it argues the
point better than any rule could. It is the guard that checks whether the
`internal/session` suite disturbed the checkout it ran in.

I tripped it myself on 2026-09-20 by committing a change note while the suite
was running in the same tree. This is what it printed, verbatim:

```
session tests changed the checkout they were running in (/home/santosh/src/c374-land):
it stood on 43e95a26f8ff and now stands on f08536cadf59; what was committed on top of it:
	f08536cad docs: change note for the landing your-call fix
a git command ran against a repository the suite does not own, by one of two roads. Either it was
given no working directory at all, which exec reads as this process's own (task_run.go's gitWith,
#402); or it was given a directory it does own whose ground resolved to the repository ABOVE it
[...] Which one it was, this guard cannot tell you; if the run had GOTMPDIR or TMPDIR pointing
inside a checkout, suspect the second. Undo the above before pushing.
(a second checkout running this same suite beside you cannot cause this; a test that names no
directory can [...] When this checkout is a linked worktree of a shared clone, branch churn is not
reported at all [...] a leak that only cut a task/ branch from inside a linked worktree slips past
here, and the head and the porcelain above are what catch it.)
```

Set it beside every instance above and the contrast is the whole subject. Those
are one output with two meanings. This is:

1. ONE MEANING, STATED. Not "the tree changed" for somebody to work out. It
   quotes both shas and lists the commit that arrived.
2. THE RIVAL MEANING EXPLICITLY RULED OUT. "a second checkout running this same
   suite beside you cannot cause this." That is the sentence a reader would
   otherwise spend twenty minutes establishing, and it is the difference between
   a signal and an accusation.
3. THE AMBIGUITY THAT REMAINS, NAMED AS AMBIGUITY. "Which one it was, this guard
   cannot tell you", followed by the one reading that separates the two roads.
   It does not pick the likelier cause and present it as the cause.
4. ITS OWN BLIND SPOT DECLARED. It says which leak slips past it, and what does
   catch that one instead.

Point 4 is the one worth copying hardest, because it is the opposite of every
defect in this issue. A test that cannot fail is silent about what it does not
cover. This guard's failure output states what it does not cover, so the next
person does not mistake its silence for coverage.

The rule it suggests is not "avoid ambiguous signals", which nobody can act on.
It is: WHEN A CHECK FIRES, SAY WHICH CAUSE, RULE OUT THE INNOCENT ONE, NAME WHAT
YOU STILL CANNOT DISTINGUISH, AND SAY WHERE YOU ARE BLIND. Four sentences of
output, written once, against an indefinite number of confused readings later.

(The block above is quoted exactly as the tool printed it, including its
punctuation, because misquoting evidence to satisfy a prose rule would be the
worse error. My own text carries none.)

issue.title: connect: the Slack thread limit is written down once

repository.name: CodeAF
repository.description: Open-Source Software factory for Open Models

issue.body:
The number 15 was written down three times for one limit:

- `SlackReadThread`'s doc, as the word "fifteen"
- the `limit` query parameter, as `"15"`, which is the one that actually applies it
- the tool description a model reads, as `"15"`, in a different package

The third is the one that goes stale in silence. If somebody changes the limit, the call still returns whatever Slack returns and the model still believes whatever the sentence said, so nothing fails and nobody finds out. `connect.SlackThreadLimit` is now the one place and both sites reference it. This is CLAUDE.md's one-source-of-truth rule, whose own worked example is the `propose_task` 40/200 pair.

**The description is still a compile-time const.** Both operands are string constants, so `"Read one Slack thread in order, up to " + connect.SlackThreadLimit + " messages. ..."` folds at compile time. Nothing moved into `init`, the declaration stays usable everywhere a const is, and the rendered text is byte for byte what it was:

```
Read one Slack thread in order, up to 15 messages. The channel id and ts are the final line of a slack_search result; ...
```

`internal/session` already imported `internal/connect`, so no new edge.

**No test.** A `strings.Contains(slackReadThreadDescription, connect.SlackThreadLimit)` assertion would hold for every possible value of either side and could never fail. The compile-time concatenation is the mechanism; a test on top of it would be a test that cannot fail, which is the shape #1306 is about.

### The settings rule that rides with it

`Setting.read` now states the same argument where it has teeth. A row's `read` returns **what the product will actually use**, not what is stored: where a value passes through a resolver, the row reads the resolver, so a person who types something the resolver will not honour watches it change in front of them.

That is what makes a lossy store safe, and it is the only thing that does. `persistedCount` (#1369) collapses unset and zero the moment the value is written, and nothing downstream of the row can recover the difference, because downstream never sees what was typed. The row typing the default back at the person is the whole safety argument, so it belongs on the field that does it rather than in the helper that depends on it. #1369 and this now point at each other.

### Checks

On Spark, fresh clone of `santos/dev2` at `d91bb63ae`, `~/src/wt-slack15`.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `gofmt -l ./internal ./cmd` | empty |
| `go build ./...` | 0 |
| `go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check` | 0, 100 entries well formed |
| `go test ./internal/connect ./internal/config ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw` | 0 |
| `go test ./internal/session` | ok, 249.6s |
| combined | `COMBINED_RC=0` |
| em dashes on added lines | 0 |

`internal/tui3` and `cmd/codeaf` are out of scope: neither reads the constant or the description, and neither file in them changed.
